story.head: Unstoppable force vs. immovable object
paras: The Flames (10-12-2) lost 4-3 in overtime to Chicago on Saturday, while the Senators (15-6-3) beat Los Angeles 4-2 the same night. Going in, the Flames are fifth in the Pacific (23rd in the NHL) and the Senators first in the Atlantic (tied for fourth).
The Flames’ record (.458) is about what their chances are worth. The Senators’ record (.688) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.608), largely because they’re 7-3 in one-goal games.

The Flames play some of the league’s fastest games (2nd) and have struggled on the power play (32nd). The Senators, by contrast, play slow, tight games (3rd lowest). The Flames also take a lot of low-quality shots (32nd), so good looks are likely to be hard to come by for them. Calgary has scored 2.50 goals a game, the second fewest in the league. The Senators forecheck as hard as almost anyone (2nd) and rarely get pinned in their own end (2nd). Something has to give when the Flames’ shooting runs into the Sens’ defense.

Joel Farabee (7 G / 11 A / 18 P in 24 GP) leads the Flames in scoring, and Matt Coronato (5 G / 11 A / 16 P in 24 GP) isn’t far behind. Tim Stützle (13 G / 18 A / 31 P in 24 GP) leads the Senators in scoring and is tied for tenth in the NHL, with eight points in his last five games. Drake Batherson (12 G / 10 A / 22 P in 24 GP) isn’t far behind.
Devin Cooley (5-5-0 / .905 SV% in 10 GS) is expected to go for Calgary. Linus Ullmark (11-1-0 / .937 SV% in 12 GS) has been outstanding for Ottawa and is expected to start.

At home, Travis Green likes to send Blais, Halliday and Cousins out against opponents’ fourth lines, so watch for them against Tsyplakov, Castagna and Suniev. Elsewhere, the Senators usually control more of the chances than the Flames do.
